claims.text: The starting Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
The as-manufactured FCC matrix is a supersaturated solid solution.
The starting alloy has a fairly uniform elemental distribution and minimal detrimental precipitates or grain-boundary segregation.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by selective reactions at grain boundaries.
Oxidizing exposure preferentially oxidizes reactive elements such as Cr and Ti.
Preferential oxidation of Cr and Ti occurs specifically at grain boundaries.
Selective grain-boundary reactions deplete Cr and Ti from the alloy matrix.
Local elemental depletion promotes nucleation of brittle sigma phase.
Selective oxidation produces discontinuous, nonadherent intergranular oxide scales.
Reducing exposure can induce grain-boundary precipitation.
Elevated temperature enhances diffusion of reactive species.
Brittle precipitates and intergranular oxides lower grain-boundary cohesion.
Loss of grain-boundary cohesion promotes rapid crack initiation and catastrophic propagation.
Inert or mildly reducing conditions suppress the proposed grain-boundary reaction processes and preserve grain-boundary integrity.
At otherwise matched exposure conditions, high-oxygen specimens will develop thicker and possibly more discontinuous oxide layers than inert or reducing controls.
High-oxygen exposure will increase grain-boundary sigma-phase precipitation relative to inert or reducing exposure.
The proposed microstructural changes will reduce ductility and fracture toughness and cause earlier crack initiation.
The proposed behavior applies approximately from 800 to 1000 °C when reactive potential and exposure duration are sufficient for diffusion-controlled reactions.
Al may have only a minor modifying effect on oxidation kinetics.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis allows reduction-induced precipitation as a degradation route, whereas the mechanism states that reducing conditions suppress the relevant processes and preserve grain-boundary integrity.

The mechanism groups reducing and inert atmospheres as suppressive controls, but the boundary statement invokes reactive potential for 'reduction-driven effects,' leaving the expected role of reducing gas internally inconsistent.
